newsitem.title: INDIA: India calm on Pakistan, calls it internal affair.
newsitem.headline: India calm on Pakistan, calls it internal affair.

text.p: India reacted calmly on Tuesday to the dismissal of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto in Pakistan, saying it was an internal affair that would not affect ties.
"We see these events as Pakistan's internal developments and are following them closely," Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said in Zimbabwe, where he was attending a trade summit meeting.
"India has always been keen to maintain good neighbourly relations with Pakistan. This policy continues," he added in a brief statement.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence from Britain in 1947, two of them over the Himalayan region of Kashmir.
They have not held official talks for more than two years.
A defence official in New Delhi said: "If our assessment is correct, the Pakistani government would not have been dismissed without the army's blessing."
"Our perception is that the current army leadership in Pakistan does not favour military adventurism against India," the official said.

Pakistani President Farooq Leghari dismissed Bhutto's government on Tuesday, accusing it of corruption and misrule in what appears to have been a planned action that had army support and was within his constitutional powers.
The military kept a low profile. But political observers said the president could not have acted without the approval and cooperation of the generals.
Indian diplomats said they did not expect an interim governnment in Pakistan to resume talks, mainly over Kashmir.
"It is not Pakistani governments but the Pakistani establishment that determines ties with India," one diplomat told Reuters. "That establishment remains very much intact."
An Indian interior ministry official said the change in Pakistan was unlikely to make any difference to India.

"Basically, the situation will not affect us in any important way. If the government has been dismissed to check instability, and if fresh elections are held soon, we have no worries," the official said.

Former Indian foreign secretary Jyotindra Nath Dixit, the last Indian official to hold formal talks with Pakistan, said Bhutto's dismissal followed a growing list of complaints against her, including a troubled economy.
Dixit said he had known Pakistan's army chief, General Jehangir Karamat, during his time as Indian high commissioner (ambassador) in Islamabad.
"It seems that Farooq Leghari and Karamat will rule the roost," he said.
He said Karamat did not appear to be an anti-India militarist.
"He was not the sort of person who would try to seek a military solution to the problems with India," Dixit added.
